title: A Centurion's Faith, a Widow's Son, and a Forgiven Woman
summary: Jesus heals the servant of a Gentile centurion whose faith surpasses anything he has found in Israel, and at Nain he raises a widow's only son. From prison John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the one to come; Jesus points to his works and honors John as more than a prophet. At a Pharisee's dinner a sinful woman anoints his feet, and Jesus tells a parable of two debtors to show why the forgiven love much.
story: The Sermon on the Plain described the kingdom's way of life. This chapter shows who actually receives the kingdom, and the answer keeps surprising: a Roman officer, a grieving widow, tax collectors who accepted John's baptism, and a woman known in town as a sinner. Meanwhile, the respectable reject God's purpose. Luke also settles an important question at this stage: John had announced a coming one who would baptize with Spirit and fire, and Jesus' ministry of healing and mercy is not what everyone expected. Jesus answers with Isaiah's own descriptions of the age of salvation.
historical:
A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. In Capernaum, part of Herod Antipas's territory, he was probably in Antipas's service, though such units were organized on Roman lines and often recruited from non-Jews. Some Gentiles in this period admired Judaism, attended synagogues, and supported them without becoming full converts; Luke will call such people God-fearers in Acts. This centurion's gift of a synagogue fits that pattern. Matthew 8:5-13 tells the same healing more briefly, with the centurion approaching Jesus directly; Luke describes him sending Jewish elders and then friends, a way of saying the same request came through agents.

Nain was a village in lower Galilee, a few miles southeast of Nazareth, near where the Old Testament town of Shunem stood. At Shunem Elisha had raised a woman's son (2 Kings 4), and Elijah had raised the son of a widow at Zarephath (1 Kings 17). John, meanwhile, was in prison under Antipas (3:19-20); Josephus places his imprisonment at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Matthew 11:2-19 records the same exchange with John's disciples.
cultural:
A widow who lost her only son lost her protector and her means of support in a society where women seldom owned land or earned wages; the crowd following the bier would have understood the scale of her loss. Burial took place on the day of death, outside the town, and the body was carried on an open bier. Touching it made a person ritually unclean.

At formal dinners guests reclined on couches or cushions, leaning on the left elbow, with their feet stretched out away from the table. That is how the woman could stand behind Jesus at his feet. Such meals in a notable person's house were semi-public, and uninvited people could come in to watch. A host normally offered water for guests' dusty feet, greeted them with a kiss, and might offer oil for the head; Simon gave none of these. A woman letting down her hair in public was considered immodest, so her act was costly in reputation as well as in perfume. A denarius was roughly a day's wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:2), so the larger debt was more than a year's work.
literary: The chapter builds carefully toward the question of verse 49, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” The two opening miracles mirror the stories of Elijah and Elisha that Jesus mentioned at Nazareth (4:25-27): a Gentile helped, a widow's son raised and, in words that echo 1 Kings 17:23, given back to his mother. Jesus' reply to John (verse 22) gathers phrases from Isaiah 35 and 61. The children's game in verses 31-35 (one group pipes a wedding tune or a funeral dirge and the other refuses to play) is a parable of a generation that finds fault with every messenger. The dinner scene contains a parable inside a story, then an application that contrasts Simon's hospitality point by point with the woman's.

outline.t: The widow's son raised at Nain
A sinful woman anoints Jesus at Simon's table

doctrines.note: The centurion trusts that Jesus' word has authority at a distance, as a commander's word does. The woman's faith saves her. In both cases faith is humble reliance on Jesus rather than a claim of worthiness.
The woman is forgiven, saved, and sent in peace. Her love is the fruit of forgiveness, not its price: Jesus' parable says the one forgiven more loves more, not that love earns forgiveness.
Raising the widow's son is a sign of the resurrection hope that runs through Scripture: God is able to give life back. The crowd rightly says that God has visited his people.

words.note: Splagchnizomai, to have compassion, from a word for the inner organs, where ancient people located deep feeling. In the Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus or of characters in his parables who act like God, such as the Samaritan (10:33) and the father of the lost son (15:20).

Dikaioo, to justify or declare right. In verse 29 the people acknowledged God's justice, literally justified God, by accepting John's baptism. In verse 35 wisdom is justified by her children. The word describes a verdict, not a moral improvement.

Sozo, to save, rescue, or heal. Luke uses it of physical healing and of forgiveness and restored relationship with God. Here it sums up what has happened to the woman: forgiven, accepted, and sent in peace.

christ: This chapter answers John's question from many sides. Jesus is the one whose word heals at a distance, whose touch reverses death, and who acts with a compassion that goes to the grieving widow before anyone asks. Luke calls him the Lord in verse 13, the first time the narrator uses that title of the earthly Jesus in the story of his ministry. He is more than the great prophet the crowd sees: he fulfills what Isaiah said God himself would do, and he forgives sins on his own authority. His answer to John also contains a gentle warning, “Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.” Jesus is not always the Messiah people expect, and blessing belongs to those who trust him anyway.

hard.q: Why would John the Baptist, who baptized Jesus and heard the voice from heaven, doubt whether he was the one?
hard.a: Interpreters answer this differently. Many think John's question is genuine: he had announced a coming one with an axe and winnowing fork, who would baptize with fire and burn the chaff, and he now sat in Herod's prison while Jesus healed, ate with sinners, and did not bring judgment on the wicked. A prophet can be certain of his calling and still puzzled about how God is fulfilling it. Some older interpreters held that John asked for the sake of his disciples, to point them to Jesus, though the text says John sent to ask. Jesus neither rebukes John nor gives a simple yes; he points to deeds that match Isaiah's promises and then praises John publicly. The answer suggests that judgment is real but that the first coming of the Messiah is marked by mercy, with the harvest still to come.

questions: The centurion says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof. How does his humility compare with the elders' argument that he is worthy?
Jesus says the one forgiven little loves little. Do you think of yourself more as Simon or as the woman?
John struggled when Jesus did not act as he expected. When has God's way of working disappointed or puzzled you, and what helped you keep trusting?
